result: DNa01 and DNa02 project to leg neuromeres in the ventral nerve cord, forming selective connections onto leg-control networks. DNa02 makes more direct synaptic connections onto motor neurons compared to DNa01, and very few postsynaptic cells are shared between the two DN types.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge these anatomical findings without challenge. The editor notes the work characterizes 'two types of descending neurons (DNs) that connect the brain to motor units,' and Reviewer 3 highlights the connectome data showing 'largely non-overlapping outputs in the ventral nerve cord.' These anatomical claims are accepted as foundational to the study.

result: Both DNa01 and DNa02 are depolarized before ipsilateral steering and hyperpolarized when the fly stops moving. DNa02 exhibits more transient fluctuations and is recruited earlier than DNa01, with spike rate fluctuations in DNa02 typically preceding those in DNa01.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 praises the 'technically impressive' in-vivo recordings and notes that 'DNa02 predicts transient turns DNa01 predicts slow sustained turns.' Reviewer 1 describes the experiments as 'well-designed and controlled.' The temporal dynamics and differential recruitment patterns are accepted as compelling evidence for distinct functional roles.

result: DNa01 and DNa02 firing rate increases are followed by changes in rotational and sideways velocity but not consistently in forward velocity. Steering filters are larger for DNa02 than DNa01, suggesting DNa02 operates with higher gain. DNa02 filters are biphasic while DNa01 filters are monophasic, indicating DNa02 produces more transient steering changes and provides better behavioral predictions.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 emphasizes that the recordings 'provide a much higher resolution DN characterization' and notes the distinct functional profiles are well-supported. The editor highlights that the work shows DNs are 'involved in different aspects of turning control.' These filter analyses and gain differences are accepted as key evidence for functional specialization.

result: Rotational velocity is consistently related to the difference in right-left DNa02 firing rates in a linear relationship across the dynamic range, consistent during both forward and backward walking. Similar results were obtained for DNa01. Predictions from simultaneously recorded right-left pairs accurately predict turns in both directions.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 specifically highlights the 'simultaneous recordings from bilateral DNs (Fig. 3)' as 'especially impressive,' noting they 'show clearly that DNa02 cells not only fire more during ipsilateral turning events but that they get inhibited during contralateral turns.' Reviewer 2 emphasizes the importance of the statement that 'DNa02 activity was higher on the side ipsilateral to the attractive stimulus, but contralateral to the aversive stimulus' as 'really important - and only possible to see because of the dual recordings.'

result: Micro-stimulating PEN1 neurons causes EPG bump jumps, followed by compensatory behavioral turns in the correct direction to return the bump via the shortest path. DNa02 fires bursts before compensatory turns, predicts trial-to-trial variability in turn magnitude, and is recruited specifically on the side predicting turn direction. This demonstrates DNa02 activity predicts steering maneuvers guided by the head direction system.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 describes the 'experiment in Figure 4' as 'elegant' and notes the authors 'put a lot of effort into ensuring that ATP puffs do not accidentally activate the DNs.' Reviewer 3 calls this 'another technical feat' that 'provided a way to causally relate changes in the head-direction system to DNa02 activity.' The editor notes the work shows 'orientation signals act by preferentially increasing relative stimulation onto left- or right-turn-inducing DNs.'

result: Lateralized fictive odor stimuli produce asymmetric DNa02 responses with higher firing on the ipsilateral side and contralateral hyperpolarization, while fictive heat stimuli produce higher firing contralateral to the stimulus. DNa02 activity is higher ipsilateral to attractive stimuli but contralateral to aversive stimuli, encoding the laterality of the stimulus-evoked action rather than the stimulus itself. DNa02 is activated ~150ms before stimulus-evoked turns and predicts trial-to-trial variability.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 specifically highlights the finding that 'DNa02 activity was higher on the side ipsilateral to the attractive stimulus, but contralateral to the aversive stimulus' as 'really important.' Reviewer 2 also notes the 'idea that different sensory cues can converge on a common motor program' where 'the turn-toward or turn-away mechanism is initiated by valence rather than whether the stimulus was odor or temperature' is 'of particular interest.'

result: DNa02 hyperpolarizes when the fly stops walking but continues responding to lateralized odors during immobility with similar stimulus-evoked firing rate changes as during walking. This suggests DNa02 contains information about latent steering drives even in quiescent behavioral states.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these observations about latent activity. The findings are consistent with the broader acceptance of DNa02's role in encoding steering commands, and no concerns are raised about the interpretation of activity during immobility.

result: The inputs to DNa02 are largely non-overlapping with those of DNa01, and they have largely non-overlapping outputs in the ventral nerve cord. Both receive substantial input from central brain intrinsic neurons, but only DNa02 receives direct input from PFL3 cells. This suggests they represent parallel and largely independent pathways for steering control.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes that 'connectome data shows these two DNs receive largely non-overlapping inputs in the brain, and they have largely non-overlapping outputs in the ventral nerve cord.' The editor acknowledges the work characterizes DNs 'involved in different aspects of turning control.' These connectome findings are accepted as supporting the functional specialization observed in electrophysiology.

result: PFL3 cells compare head direction with internal goal signals and produce directional steering commands when mismatched. PFL3 neurons are the likely origin of turning signals in DNa02 during head direction system perturbations. PFL3 sends both direct and strong indirect projections to DNa02 via DNa03 and LAL010, and also projects to cells that inhibit contralateral copies of DNa02, DNa03, and LAL010. This architecture suggests a 'see-saw' model of steering with opposite effects on the two copies of DNa02.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes that 'the insights on the pre-synaptic side - how sensory and central complex heading circuits converge onto these DNs is stronger' than motor-side insights. Reviewer 2 also comments that 'the "see-saw", where left-right symmetry is broken to allow a turn, presumably by excitation on one side and inhibition of the other leg motor modules, is interesting but not well explained here.' While the see-saw mechanism needs better explanation, the connectivity patterns themselves are accepted.

result: Some indirect connections onto DNa02 are bilaterally symmetric. DNa03 and LAL010 receive strong bilaterally symmetric projections from PFL2, which is recruited when the fly is oriented away from its internal goal and increases overall steering gain without specifying turn direction.
evaluation: These connectome findings are presented alongside the see-saw model and are not challenged by reviewers. They are accepted as part of the broader connectivity analysis showing how different pathways contribute to steering control.

result: Multiple pathways connect olfactory and thermosensory peripheral cells to DNa02, with the shortest involving MBON32. MBON32 projections are organized for see-saw steering and could drive turning toward appetitive stimuli or away from aversive stimuli. This is explained by parallel plastic excitatory and fixed inhibitory pathways to MBON32, where depression of KC→MBON32 synapses by aversive stimuli unmasks inhibition.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes the 'idea that different sensory cues can converge on a common motor program' is 'of particular interest.' The connectome-based model for valence-dependent steering through MBON32 plasticity is accepted as consistent with the experimental observations of opposite DNa02 responses to attractive versus aversive stimuli.

result: DNa02 receives abundant visual input from multiple sources: visual projection neurons from the optic lobe, projection neurons in the anterior optic tubercle downstream from LC10 cells (small object motion detectors), and via MBON32 which receives visual input in addition to olfactory and thermosensory input.
evaluation: These connectome findings are not challenged by reviewers and are accepted as part of the comprehensive characterization of DNa02 inputs showing integration of multiple sensory modalities.

result: DNa02 is a site of integration for many steering control pathways, which tend to be arranged for see-saw steering control (when one copy is excited, the other is inhibited). Many pathways involve parallel excitation and inhibition, which could provide a mechanism to specify steering direction based on E/I balance.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes the see-saw model is 'interesting but not well explained here' and that 'how hyperpolarization affects motor outputs is not clear.' However, the basic connectivity patterns supporting the see-saw architecture are accepted. The mechanistic details need clarification, but the anatomical organization is not disputed.

result: Unilateral optogenetic activation of DNa02 evoked a small but statistically significant steering bias in the ipsilateral direction, larger than expected by chance.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these optogenetic activation results. Reviewer 2 notes the 'gain-of-function experiments in freely walking flies' are part of the technically impressive dataset. The modest effect size is consistent with the interpretation that DNa02 is one of many steering DNs.

result: Inhibiting DNa01 significantly reduced sideways speed and produced defects in inner-back-leg stance prolongation, while rotational speed was unchanged when either DNa01 or DNa02 were inhibited. A similar trend for stance prolongation defects was observed with DNa02 inhibition but fell short of statistical significance. This suggests defects in specific leg maneuvers are compensated via other mechanisms to achieve normal body rotation.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes that 'loss-of-function was tested but has minimal effect, which is not surprising in a system with partially redundant control mechanisms.' Reviewer 3 acknowledges that 'optogenetic activation or inactivation showed relatively subtle phenotypes for both neurons (consistent with data in other recent preprints, Yang et al 2023 and Feng et al 2024).' The modest loss-of-function effects are accepted as consistent with redundancy in the steering system.

result: Inhibiting either DNa01 or DNa02 altered leg movement rhythm (increased step length, decreased step frequency) regardless of walking direction. Inhibiting DNa01 also decreased forward velocity.
evaluation: These effects on leg kinematics are not challenged by reviewers and are accepted as part of the loss-of-function phenotype characterization. They contribute to understanding how these DNs influence motor output.

result: DNa01 and DNa02 are both recruited during turning bouts in walking flies, but have distinct functional profiles: DNa02 predicts large, rapid, transient steering events and is recruited earlier, while DNa01 predicts smaller, slower steering events. These results argue that the two DNs play specialized roles in steering control.
evaluation: The editor states the work shows DNs are 'involved in different aspects of turning control.' Reviewer 3 notes the 'electrophysiological results in this study support this hypothesis: these two DN types have distinct functional profiles.' The functional specialization is accepted as a major finding, though Reviewer 3 notes 'the role of DNa01 on the other hand seems unclear based on physiology, optogenetics perturbations as well as connectome analysis.'

result: Optogenetically inhibiting DNa01 produced only small defects in steering, and inhibiting DNa02 did not produce statistically significant effects on steering.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states this is 'not surprising in a system with partially redundant control mechanisms.' Reviewer 3 notes these results are 'consistent with data in other recent preprints, Yang et al 2023 and Feng et al 2024.' The modest loss-of-function effects are accepted as expected given the redundancy in the steering system.

result: Subsequent studies (Yang et al. 2023, Feng et al. 2024, Braun et al. 2024) confirmed key findings: unilateral DNa02 excitation produces ipsilateral rotation, bilateral DNa02 ablation reduces corrective turning velocity, bilateral activation can drive turning in either direction, and DNa02 perturbation mainly affects ipsilateral leg movements. The brain connectome analyses explain how DNa02 activity correlates with both ipsi- and contralateral legs through see-saw arrangement. DNa01 and DNa02 are normally recruited for steering control, though bilateral perturbations can produce forward velocity changes.
evaluation: The editor explicitly notes 'these compelling results, together with the independent work that they have inspired, represent significant progress.' Reviewer 2 states the 'data is also consistent with/complementary to subsequent manuscripts (Yang 2023, Feng 2024, and Ros 2024).' The convergence of findings across multiple independent studies strongly supports the main conclusions.
